clinicalPearls: A chronic, slowly progressive, distal and predominantly sensory demyelinating neuropathy caused by IgM antibodies against myelin-associated glycoprotein.
Presents in older adults with sensory ataxia, distal paraesthesiae and a characteristic prominent postural or action tremor of the hands.
Almost always associated with an IgM monoclonal gammopathy, so serum immunofixation and protein electrophoresis are mandatory.

The phenotype is classically distal, acquired and demyelinating, sometimes labelled distal acquired demyelinating symmetric neuropathy, and progresses far more slowly than chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy.
Nerve conduction studies show disproportionately prolonged distal motor latencies, reflected in a raised terminal latency index, a signature of distal-predominant demyelination.
Unlike chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy, it usually responds poorly to corticosteroids, intravenous immunoglobulin and plasma exchange.
Anti-MAG antibodies react with the HNK-1 carbohydrate epitope, detectable by ELISA, and titres support but do not alone confirm the diagnosis.
Investigate for an underlying B-cell lymphoproliferative disorder such as Waldenstrom macroglobulinaemia; B-cell depletion is the mainstay when treatment is warranted.
reference.pathophysiology: Anti-MAG neuropathy is a humorally mediated demyelinating disorder in which a monoclonal IgM paraprotein, typically of kappa light-chain type, is directed against myelin-associated glycoprotein, a minor adhesion molecule concentrated in periaxonal and paranodal Schwann-cell membranes that shares the HNK-1 carbohydrate epitope with other peripheral nerve glycoconjugates. The antibody penetrates the endoneurium and deposits on the outermost myelin lamellae, fixing complement and causing a distinctive widening of the myelin lamellae seen on electron microscopy. This disrupts the axon-Schwann-cell interaction essential for stable myelin, producing segmental demyelination that is most pronounced in the longest, most distal nerve fibres and preferentially affecting large sensory fibres, which accounts for the prominent sensory ataxia and relative sparing of strength early in the disease. Progressive secondary axonal loss develops over years and correlates with fixed disability. Because the causative clone is a low-grade B-cell population, the disorder sits within the spectrum of IgM-related lymphoproliferative disease, and the slow, indolent tempo distinguishes it mechanistically from the more inflammatory, T-cell-influenced chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy.
additionalDifferentials: Vitamin B12 deficiency with sensory ataxia
additionalInvestigations: Serum protein electrophoresis with immunofixation to detect and type the IgM paraprotein
Nerve conduction studies with calculation of the terminal latency index
Serum immunoglobulins, free light chains and cryoglobulins
Bone marrow examination when a lymphoproliferative disorder is suspected
MYD88 mutation testing where Waldenstrom macroglobulinaemia is considered
Sural nerve biopsy in selected atypical cases showing widened myelin lamellae
redFlags: Rapidly progressive weakness rather than the expected indolent sensory course, suggesting an alternative diagnosis
Systemic features such as weight loss, organomegaly or lymphadenopathy pointing to lymphoproliferative disease
Hyperviscosity symptoms including visual disturbance and mucosal bleeding with high IgM levels
Marked autonomic dysfunction or prominent pain suggesting amyloidosis
New bone pain or oedema raising the possibility of POEMS syndrome
reference.prognosis: The neuropathy is usually indolent, and although many patients remain ambulant for years, gradual axonal loss produces slowly accumulating sensory ataxia and disability; treatment responses are often modest and incomplete. The outlook is also shaped by any underlying lymphoproliferative disorder.
pitfalls: Mistaking the disorder for chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy and expecting a good response to immunoglobulin or steroids
Failing to perform immunofixation and missing the associated IgM paraprotein
Attributing the hand tremor to a primary movement disorder rather than the neuropathy
Overtreating stable, minimally symptomatic disease with aggressive immunosuppression
Not screening for Waldenstrom macroglobulinaemia and other B-cell malignancies
references: Bradley and Daroff's Neurology in Clinical Practice
Peripheral nerve society guideline on paraproteinaemic demyelinating neuropathies
management: Reserve treatment for progressive disability, using rituximab directed against the IgM-producing B-cell clone as the best-evidenced option
Investigate and treat the underlying IgM monoclonal gammopathy or lymphoproliferative disorder such as Waldenstrom macroglobulinaemia, with haematology involvement
Avoid reliance on corticosteroids, intravenous immunoglobulin and plasma exchange, which are usually ineffective in this neuropathy
Physiotherapy and occupational therapy for sensory ataxia, gait and the disabling action tremor, with assistive devices
Manage neuropathic symptoms and institute falls-prevention measures
Long-term monitoring of the paraprotein and clinical progression with joint neurology-haematology follow-up
